PM says Prof. Prasad to be sworn-in next week as Deputy PM and Minister for Employment
item.description: Vijay Narayan , Karishma Kumari · 13/11/2026 Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka says National Federation Party Leader, Professor Biman Prasad, will be sworn-in as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations next week when Government House is ready.
item.content:encoded:
Vijay Narayan , Karishma Kumari · 13/11/2026

Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka says National Federation Party Leader, Professor Biman Prasad, will be sworn-in as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations next week when Government House is ready.

However, Professor Prasad has said that because of the NFP's current disagreement over the Constitution Amendment Bill, he needs to carefully consider whether he would return to cabinet at this stage.

Speaking to fijivillage News today, Prime Minister Rabuka who was earlier in Vanua Levu, says he is in the western division now.

Rabuka says he asked the office to arrange for Professor Prasad's swearing-in today but President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu is busy in the west.

When asked on whether there will be any conditions before Professor Prasad is reappointed as a cabinet minister and Deputy Prime Minister as Professor Prasad has made it clear that he will vote against the Constitution Amendment Bill and wants further consultations after the general elections, Rabuka says there will be no conditions.

Rabuka says if Professor Prasad says he will vote against the Constitution Bill, any action taken can only be the 'result' of that vote, not the 'intention' to vote that way.

When contacted by fijivillage News today, Professor Prasad says he has not heard from the Prime Minister at all.

Professor Biman Prasad who was the former Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance, was acquitted of both charges in his FICAC case after the court found that the prosecution had failed to prove an essential element of the alleged offences.

Magistrate Yogesh Prasad found that FICAC had failed to establish that Professor Prasad was legally an office holder under the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Act 2013.

He said the definition of an office holder under Section 2 of the Act specifically lists the president, vice-president, treasurer, secretary and registered officers of a political party, but does not include the position of party leader.

The court also heard that FICAC relied on the argument that Professor Prasad was an office holder because he had been appointed as the NFP leader, with the prosecution referring to a letter dated 3rd June 2014 and the party's constitution.

Magistrate Prasad said that FICAC had also argued that Section 2 of the Act should be interpreted to include a party leader who was elected through the party's internal processes.

However, the defence had challenged this interpretation, submitting that there was no evidence that Professor Prasad was appointed or elected to any of the positions specifically recognised as office holders under the Act.

He said the defence also argued that the position of party leader was not included in the legal definition of an office holder under the legislation.

Magistrate Prasad said the plain and literal meaning of the law had to be applied and that the court could not add to or alter the wording of the legislation.

He said extending the definition of office holder to include a party leader, when the position was not expressly listed in the Act, would not be justified.

Referring to Section 5(3)(a) and (b) of the Act, which sets out the qualifications and disqualifications for individuals serving as office holders of registered political parties, Magistrate Prasad concluded that the prosecution had failed to prove that Professor Prasad was an office holder, which was an essential ingredient of both the main charge and the alternative count.

The no case to answer ruling followed the closure of the prosecution's case after FICAC called three witnesses.

item.title: Drivers warned to exercise caution near Nabou bush fire in Nadi
item.description: Temalesi Vono , Vijay Narayan · 13/11/2026 A bush fire has been reported at Nabou in Nadi along Queens Highway, with drivers advised to exercise caution when travelling in the area.
item.content:encoded:
Temalesi Vono , Vijay Narayan · 13/11/2026

A bush fire has been reported at Nabou in Nadi along Queens Highway, with drivers advised to exercise caution when travelling in the area.

When contacted, the National Fire Authority in Nadi confirmed the bush fire and says its trucks are currently attending to another grass fire before proceeding to Nabou.

Drivers are urged to remain cautious while travelling through the area.

The National Fire Authority is raising concerns over the increasing number of fire incidents across the Western Division amid the current El Niño conditions, which are contributing to drier weather and heightened fire risks.

They say a recent bushfire on a mountain near Togavere Village, between Rakiraki and Tavua, is a reminder of how quickly fires can spread under dry conditions, threatening nearby communities, vegetation and properties.

The public is strongly advised to take extra precautions to prevent fires, including avoid burning rubbish, dry grass and garden waste, do not throw burning cigarette butts into bushes or roadside areas, avoid lighting open fires near dry vegetation, never leave fires unattended, properly extinguish any fire after use and report any uncontrolled fire immediately.

Stay alert. Stay safe. Help prevent fires.

item.title: People First warns against rushing Constitution Bill, wants BLV excluded from Senate and presidential appointment
item.description: The People First Party is warning against rushing the Constitution Amendment Bill, saying citizens must be given sufficient time to understand the proposed changes and their implications before any decision is made. Presenting the party's submission to the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill, People First representative Rinesh Sharma says the party deliberately cho
item.content:encoded:
The People First Party is warning against rushing the Constitution Amendment Bill, saying citizens must be given sufficient time to understand the proposed changes and their implications before any decision is made.

Presenting the party's submission to the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill, People First representative Rinesh Sharma says the party deliberately chose not to participate in the Constitution Review Commission process from the beginning because it disputed the correctness and legitimacy of the process.

Sharma stresses that the party's participation in the parliamentary special committee does not mean it supports the Bill.

Sharma warns that rushing the constitutional process could harm the country , saying changing or drafting a Constitution is one of the most important tasks a nation can undertake and should not be treated like ordinary legislation.

Sharma says hurried debates and short deadlines deprive citizens of the time needed to read, understand and discuss the proposed changes.

He says the 150-page Bill, containing 229 clauses and complex legal language, creates a barrier for ordinary citizens trying to understand their rights and how the proposed changes could affect their lives.

Sharma says widespread public awareness, advocacy and civic education programmes must be conducted before any vote takes place.

He says major constitutional changes should be decided through a referendum rather than Parliament having the final say.

Sharma says a referendum would give every eligible voter an equal opportunity to approve or reject changes to the country's supreme law.

He also warns against concentrating power in one person or a small group, saying when people lose their say in how fundamental rules are made, democracy exists only in name.

On the proposed recognition of the Bose Levu Vakaturaga, People First says it respects the traditional chiefly system but believes its role should remain focused on customary and traditional leadership rather than national governance.

The party says governance should remain with democratically elected representatives and that traditional structures should not override democratic principles of equality and inclusive representation.

People First representative Arista Bosei says the appointment of the President should return to the 2013 Constitution, under which the Prime Minister and Leader of the Opposition each nominate a candidate for Parliament to vote on.

He recommends that every political party represented in Parliament should also be allowed to nominate a candidate.

Bosei says the President, as Head of State, must represent all citizens equally, while the BLV represents a single community.

Bosei says restricting presidential nominations to the BLV effectively limits the office to hereditary chiefly ranks, permanently excluding ordinary iTaukei citizens and all other Fijians from aspiring to the nation's highest office on the basis of merit, service and capability.

Opposition MP Sachida Nand challenged the party's interpretation, saying there was no provision in the draft Bill stating that the BLV must appoint someone with chiefly rank as President.

Rinesh Sharma says the party is concerned about possible interpretations arising from what it considers ambiguous provisions in the Bill and believes it is important to consider potential scenarios where provisions are not clearly defined.

Attorney General Sevuloni Valenitabua also questioned the party's interpretation, saying the clause speaks for itself and that it appeared the party was making assumptions about the exclusion of other candidates.

People First strongly opposes the establishment of a Senate, saying Fiji cannot afford the substantial recurring financial burden.

A party representative estimates that establishing a separate institution, including its own Secretary-General, secretariat and administrative structure, would cost between $15 million and $20 million annually.

The party says if the committee nevertheless decides to establish a Senate, its members must be democratically elected rather than appointed.

People First representative Lusia Vusanimasei recommends removing the reference to Christianity and replacing it with either 'God' or 'religion'.

She says the current wording contradicts the constitutional protection of freedom of religion, conscience and belief.

Vusanimasei also recommends retaining Fiji as a secular state rather than changing the heading of clause four to religious liberty.

She says a secular state remains neutral in matters of religion and protects both government institutions and individual beliefs.

However, Valenitabua says the Constitution Review Commission deliberately changed the heading from secular state to religious liberty following submissions received from members of the public.

Valenitabua says there was overwhelming support among citizens who made submissions for the removal of the term secular state.

He says the provisions under clause four remain unchanged and protect the religious rights of every person.

People First also wants Fiji to remain one national constituency under the 2013 electoral system.

item.title: Lautoka initiative promotes diabetes awareness and early detection
item.description: A community initiative in Lautoka is encouraging Fijians to take a more proactive approach to their health through diabetes awareness, early detection and healthier lifestyle choices. The event, held at Shirley Park, brought together the Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Diabetes Fiji and members of the public for health check-ups and a community walk.
item.content:encoded:
A community initiative in Lautoka is encouraging Fijians to take a more proactive approach to their health through diabetes awareness, early detection and healthier lifestyle choices.

The event, held at Shirley Park, brought together the Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Diabetes Fiji and members of the public for health check-ups and a community walk.

The initiative was supported by Punjas, and it highlighted the importance of regular health monitoring and early detection, while encouraging individuals and families to adopt simple lifestyle changes that can help prevent and manage diabetes and improve their overall quality of life.

Punjas says its responsibility extends beyond the products it manufactures and the business it operates, recognising its role as part of the wider Fijian community.

As part of its commitment to supporting healthier food choices, Punjas offers consumers a range of products, including Punjas Parboiled Rice, Wholemeal Flour and Wholemeal Wraps, which can form part of a balanced and varied diet.

Punjas also acknowledged the efforts of the Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Diabetes Fiji and all participating organisations in raising awareness about diabetes and encouraging healthier communities.

The company says it will continue supporting meaningful community initiatives that promote healthier lifestyles and contribute to a healthier Fiji.
